claims.feature: Shippey on delivered archaism and metre
claims.claim: Shippey remarks that Tolkien's lines are archaic though persuasive when delivered with conviction, and that Tolkien became very strict about metre.
claims.source: Writers Write, 'Talking LOTR With Tolkien Expert Professor Thomas Shippey'; Tolkien Library Shippey chat

claims.claim: The LotR narrator's voice shifts with circumstance and with which characters are present, from the comic fox aside in the Shire to darker, unsettling prose once the hobbits leave it.
claims.quote: A fox passing through the wood on business of his own

claims.claim: Gandalf's telling of Isildur's death uses paratactic clause structure and unfamiliar proper nouns to sound sombre and chronicle-like.
claims.quote: He leaped into the waters, but the Ring slipped

claims.claim: The Prologue's subtitle 'Concerning Hobbits' adopts a nineteenth-century antiquarian register, and the early chapters carry more place-names than The Hobbit to signal expansion.

claims.feature: register shift Book IV to Book V
claims.claim: The prose rises from hobbit-colloquial in Book Four to a heroic register in the Pelennor chapters of Book Five.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings (Substack, 2026-08-12)
claims.quote: the hosts of Mordor wailed, and terror took them
claims.page: Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: After Théoden's four-stress alliterative verse, the narration itself takes on the alliterating prose rhythm of Old English writers like Ælfric and Wulfstan, resonating with the preceding verse.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: Fey he seemed, or the battle-fury of his fathers
claims.page: Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: No speaker at the Council answers in the same manner of speech as the previous one; Elrond stays consistently archaic and formal while Aragorn code-switches between Strider's plain style and his high style.
claims.source: Jaffe, The Style of the Elf-Friend (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014)
claims.quote: whose style is consistently archaic and formal

claims.claim: Glóin is characterised as curt through short, broken sentences, and each people's syntax marks its culture; alliterative verse and heroic-style prose become interchangeable when matched in register.
claims.source: MCS, Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014-04-18)
claims.page: Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose

claims.feature: iambic base shifting to alliterative metre
claims.claim: Tolkien's martial prose runs on an iambic foundation and shifts into Old English alliterative metre at the ecstatic climax of the Rohirrim's charge; the horn passage scans in both metres at once.
claims.source: Krishnan Venkatesh, Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien (2017-01-13)
claims.quote: With that he seized a great horn from Guthláf
claims.page: Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien

claims.claim: The horn-blast passage and the Rohan songs follow Anglo-Saxon alliterative patterns, so that Rohan's prose emulates Beowulf.
claims.source: David Brauer, Alliteration in The Return of the King (Gleaming Arch, 2014-09-07)
claims.quote: With that he seized a great horn
claims.page: Alliteration in The Return of the King

claims.claim: Tolkien's prose is almost entirely one-syllable native English words, preferring English coinages such as 'unlooked-for' to Latinate 'unexpectedly'.
claims.source: Mark, Goodreads discussion: Tolkien's prose, what makes it so vigorous?
claims.page: Tolkien's prose: what makes it so vigorous?

claims.claim: Tolkien's tempo is slow but never plodding, he changes mode and register seamlessly, and fast epic passages are deliberately limited so they contrast with the surrounding prose.
claims.quote: His tempo was typically slow, but never plodding.

claims.claim: A long sentence tracks difficult movement and short sentences then supply details; the Barrow-downs and Dead Marshes rely on word-sound, alliteration and understated rhyme.
claims.quote: alliteration, an understated bit of rhyme

claims.claim: The Silmarillion mixes distinct Annalistic, Antique and Appendical styles with alliterating words and rhythmical prose (citing Nagy).
claims.source: Galin, Planet Tolkien forum: Writing style/turns of phrase

claims.claim: Tolkien writes plain, clear English whose outstanding virtue is flexibility, ranging from the commonplace to the stately and sliding into metre in the Bombadil episode unnoticed; his vocabulary is not striking and has no ichor.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (1973)
claims.quote: ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

verdicts.trueWording: His actors put across their lines, archaic though they often are
verdicts.note: Quote exact, but it is Shippey's Times review of Peter Jackson's FILM: 'His actors put across their lines, archaic though they often are, with total and persuasive conviction.' The second half of the claim -- that Tolkien became very strict about metre -- appears nowhere on this page (no occurrence of metre/meter/verse re Tolkien); it must come from the unlinked 'Tolkien Library Shippey chat', which was not fetchable from the single URL given. Do not cite this page for the metre point.

verdicts.trueWording: A fox passing through the wood on business of his own
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word. Claim fully supported: 'the style of any given narrative moment depends upon its environment, both natural and characterological'; 'The voice of the narrator changes as well'; and of the post-Shire Old Forest passage, 'The tone is much darker, more unsettling, less jovial.'

verdicts.trueWording: He leaped into the waters, but the Ring slipped from his finger
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word, and the analysis is explicit: 'Note the paratactic movement from clause to clause and the introduction of unfamiliar proper nouns.' It is Gandalf's telling at Bag End. One nuance: the page's own adjectives are 'somber and sober, not antiquated but dignified' -- 'chronicle-like' is the claim's gloss, not the page's word.

Subtitle quoted verbatim and glossed as 'the stylistic mode of a certain strain of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism'. Second half also supported, via Shippey: 'there are a lot more names -- names of towns, surnames, names of regions, inns, rivers, bridges', whose effect is 'a wider, deeper, more complex world'. Minor drift: the page says names generally, not only place-names.

verdicts.trueWording: the hosts of Mordor wailed, and terror took them
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word. Claim supported: 'There is a stylistic shift as we move from Book Four to Book Five'; Book Four's language 'has been mostly hobbit-colloquial'. Small precision: the cited passage (838) is Book Five ch.5 'The Ride of the Rohirrim', which the essay says carries on 'through much of the prose describing the following battle' -- i.e. into, not from, the Pelennor chapter.

verdicts.trueWording: Fey he seemed, or the battle-fury of his fathers
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word and the claim is near-quotation of the page: Theoden's verse alliterates 'in a four-stress metrical pattern', and 'the third-person narration incorporates the related style of Old English prose, modeled by medieval writers like AElfric and Wulfstan: a prose pattern that incorporates alliteration, which resonates with the preceding verse.' Strongest-supported claim in the chunk.

verdicts.trueWording: whose style is consistently archaic and formal
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word (of Elrond, citing Shippey 70). Both other limbs supported: 'a dialogue in which no one responds in the same manner of speech as the previous speaker', and 'The easy fluctuation between Aragorn's high and dignified style (matching Boromir) and Strider's low, common style'. Post signed '--David Jaffe', April 18 2014 -- attribution correct.

Quote word-for-word: 'Gloin (and by extension dwarves) is curt, which readers in our primary reality know by his use of short, broken sentences and apposition (Shippey, 71).' Interchangeability limb is near-verbatim too: 'The alliterative verse and the heroic-style prose that follows it are interchangeable' and 'this interchangeability works as long as both are written in corresponding styles.' Post signed '-mcs'.

verdicts.trueWording: With that he seized a great horn from Guthláf his banner-bearer
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word. Every limb holds: Tolkien 'makes iambic the dominant rhythm of his martial style'; the Book Five shift is 'from straightforwardly martial to ecstatically martial'; 'This new rhythm is in fact the alliterative meter of Anglo-Saxon poetry.' The dual-scansion limb is explicit -- the horn paragraph is set out first as iambic then as alliterative, and named: 'This double-meter is how Tolkien effects an effortless, organic transition.'

verdicts.trueWording: With that he [Théoden] seized a great horn from Guthláf
verdicts.note: NOT contiguous verbatim: the blogger inserts an editorial gloss, and the page bolds each alliterating letter so the words are broken up in the source markup. Substance holds fully -- 'that alliterative element also makes its way into Tolkien's prose here', the Rohan songs are laid out with alliteration marked, and the post's thesis is that 'Tolkien's writing style emulates that of Anglo-Saxon poems', naming Beowulf (and Meduseld/Herot). Beowulf is one of two exemplars, alongside Sir Gawain.

Words identical and in order; the source carries internal quotation marks the claim drops. Full support in the same post: 'Tolkien's prose consists almost entirely of words of one syllable. Furthermore, he uses almost entirely native English words', and 'he uses English words, including words he himself coined, in place of more familiar foreign words'. Source is a 2017 forum post by 'Mark' -- an amateur reader's observation, not scholarship; weight it accordingly.

verdicts.trueWording: His tempo was typically slow, but never plodding
verdicts.note: Words identical; the claim's terminal full stop is added -- the source sentence runs on: '...but never plodding and his command of the language was sufficient that he was able to change the mode and register of his writing seamlessly'. Third limb also supported: 'passages with a fast tempo are more effective if limited and consciously contrasted with the rest of the work'.

verdicts.trueWording: alliteration, an understated bit of rhyme
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word. Both limbs on the page: 'the use of a long sentence to track the movement of characters over difficult terrain... and then a series of short sentences to describe details'. Attribution nuance: the long/short-sentence point and 'the sounds of particular words' belong to the Barrow Downs passage; 'alliteration, an understated bit of rhyme' is said of the Dead Marshes passage. The claim merges the two.

verdicts.trueWording: the Annalistic, Antique, and the Appendical
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word inside Galin's long quotation of Gergely Nagy's essay (signed 'G. Nagy'). Alliterating-words and rhythmical-prose limbs both present: 'Nearly all the alliterating words, together with the alliteration pattern itself, doubtless derive from the poem', and Old English 'rhythmical prose'. Important nuance: within Nagy's text the three-style taxonomy is credited to David Bratman -- 'which David Bratman distinguishes as' -- so 'citing Nagy' is right for the passage but Bratman owns the taxonomy.

verdicts.trueWording: It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately
verdicts.note: Quote word-for-word, and every limb of the claim is in one consecutive passage: 'Tolkien writes a plain, clear English. Its outstanding virtue is its flexibility, its variety. It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately, and can slide into metrical poetry, as in the Tom Bombadil episode, without the careless readers even noticing. Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking; he has no ichor; everything is direct, concrete, and simple.' Fetched as a PDF transcription of the 1973 essay.
